questions.question: What are Git's three main areas, in the order changes flow through them?
questions.explanation: You edit files in the working directory, select changes into the staging area with `git add`, and record the staged snapshot into the repository with `git commit`.

questions.question: What is the difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`?
options: fetch downloads and merges; pull only downloads
fetch only downloads remote refs; pull downloads and then merges (or rebases) into your branch
pull works only on the main branch
questions.explanation: fetch updates your remote-tracking refs without touching local branches — always safe. pull = fetch + merge (or + rebase with --rebase), which modifies your current branch.

questions.question: A bad commit is already pushed to the shared main branch. What's the safest way to undo it?
options: Delete the branch and recreate it
questions.explanation: revert creates a new commit that inverses the bad one — history is preserved and nobody's clones break. Force-pushing rewritten history onto a shared branch strands every collaborator (and may be blocked by branch protection).

questions.question: When is it acceptable to rebase?
options: Only on commits that haven't been shared/pushed for others to build on
questions.explanation: Rebase rewrites commit hashes. On your own unpushed (or single-author feature) branch it produces clean linear history; on shared branches it breaks everyone who pulled the old commits.

questions.question: You need to switch branches but have half-finished changes you don't want to commit. What's the standard tool?
questions.explanation: `git stash` shelves working-directory changes onto a stack; `git stash pop` restores them later. reset --hard and clean would destroy the work.

questions.question: You ran `git reset --hard HEAD~2` and lost two commits you actually needed. What recovers them?
options: git reflog to find the old HEAD, then reset/cherry-pick back to it
questions.explanation: reflog records every position HEAD has had. Find the sha from before the reset and `git reset --hard <sha>` (or cherry-pick the lost commits). Unreachable commits are kept ~90 days before garbage collection.

questions.question: `git commit --amend` changes the hash of the last commit.
questions.explanation: True. Amending creates a new commit object (new content/message/timestamp ⇒ new SHA) replacing the old tip — which is why you shouldn't amend commits already pushed to a shared branch.

questions.question: A 'fast-forward' merge creates a merge commit.
questions.explanation: False. Fast-forward simply moves the branch pointer forward when there's no divergent history — no new commit is created. Use `git merge --no-ff` to force a merge commit if your team wants explicit merge points.

questions.question: During `git rebase main`, Git stops with conflicts in two files. You fix them. What completes the rebase?
questions.explanation: During rebase you stage the resolved files and run `git rebase --continue`; Git re-applies the remaining commits. Committing manually or force-pushing mid-rebase are the classic mistakes.

questions.question: Your team wants an automated changelog and semantic-version bumps derived from commit history. Which practice enables that?
options: Conventional Commits (feat:, fix:, BREAKING CHANGE:) enforced in CI
questions.explanation: Conventional Commits give commits machine-readable types; tools like semantic-release map fix→patch, feat→minor, BREAKING CHANGE→major and generate changelogs automatically. The other options provide no parseable signal.

questions.question: Write the command to create AND switch to a new branch called hotfix/timeout (modern syntax).
questions.explanation: `git switch -c` is the modern purpose-built command; `git checkout -b` is the older equivalent that also still works.

questions.question: Write the command to interactively rebase the last 3 commits.
questions.explanation: Interactive rebase over HEAD~3 opens an editor listing the last three commits, letting you squash, reword, reorder, or drop them before they're re-applied.

questions.question: What does `git cherry-pick <sha>` do?
options: Deletes the given commit from history
Applies the changes of that single commit as a new commit on your current branch
Moves your branch pointer to that commit
questions.explanation: cherry-pick replays one commit's diff onto the current branch as a new commit (new sha). Typical use: porting a hotfix from main onto a release branch.

questions.question: In trunk-based development, feature branches typically live for weeks to keep changes isolated until fully complete.
questions.explanation: False — that describes long-lived feature branching. Trunk-based development means integrating into main at least daily via tiny branches or direct commits, with incomplete features hidden behind feature flags.
